name: David Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or political ties. This is confidential. What does a normal shift at the mine look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the loading crew at the large mine and spend most of my shift in a haul truck or walking the route before anyone starts moving rock. My technical diploma taught me the machines, but twenty years of listening to a bad bearing taught me when a screen is lying. The pay is good, and my partner and I have more than six months put away; retirement is close enough that I count shifts, though I still like teaching younger operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AI Plateau sounds like another office promise that won't move much rock. The truck still needs a driver who can feel a loose road edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved for my own job and pay, but I'd still watch the mine's maintenance budget. A quiet year can be expensive if management puts off tyres and repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the shift routine and check our retirement balance with my partner each quarter. In the first year after this modest change, I'd keep driving, record faults on the existing maintenance sheet, and add from each pay packet to retirement savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, though the mine has enough ordinary risks without a new machine story. I can see a path from these shifts into retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check with your partner first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would check whether another year of wages puts us past the pension target. My partner keeps the household accounts, and I trust that ledger more than a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which ordinary risk stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delayed tyre order worries me more than a clever office tool. I once stopped a truck after spotting a cut the inspection sheet missed.

say: **AI Plateau** would leave the haul trucks and crew routines largely as they are at the mine.
I would still say **road judgment** and tyre checks belong with trained operators.
think: My own **pay** looks secure enough to keep our retirement plan on course.
I privately worry that **maintenance cuts**, rather than AI, could make each shift less safe.
do: **Keep** leading the loading crew and recording machine faults on the current sheet.
**Review** retirement balance quarterly and add from each pay packet while shifts and wages remain steady.
feel: I feel **calm** about income, with a small, familiar concern about mine upkeep.
S0.quote: A delayed tyre order worries me more than a clever office tool.
fieldNote: His **strong savings** and senior standing make a mild AI change feel manageable for his household.
His attention returns to **tyres and roads**, the concrete safety matters he can influence each shift.

steps.text: Keep leading loading shifts and logging truck faults on the current sheet
Review retirement balance quarterly and keep adding from each pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will clean up buying and booking before it replaces anyone in a truck. The crew should get a say before software decides which repairs wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dispatch notes and parts requests could be done faster, but most of my hours are on equipment and the pit floor. I worry the younger crew might lose a route into senior work if fewer coordinators are hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union safety delegate to put any dispatch change on the meeting agenda, and I'd compare the new repair queue with what we see in the pit. In the first year I'd keep driving, but learn the approved planning screen once it is actually installed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the crew, but I don't see my own wage disappearing soon. A few years to adjust matters when retirement is near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the screen works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test one week of repair priorities before trusting the screen. The truck fault log would be my check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should hear about a missed brake warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the missed brake warning straight to the maintenance supervisor and the driver assigned to that truck. I want the driver able to stop the truck until the fault is checked.

say: **Steady Disruption** would reach buying and dispatch before the mine replaces truck operators.
I would ask for **crew review** of software decisions that affect repairs and safety.
think: My own **wage** should hold because most of my shift is hands-on equipment work.
I worry about **younger operators** losing paths into senior posts if office hiring thins.
do: **Raise** dispatch changes with the union safety delegate before software starts setting priorities.
**Learn** the approved planning screen after installation and compare its repair queue with pit reports.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the crew’s future, though my household income still looks sound.
S1.quote: The crew should get a say before software decides which repairs wait.
fieldNote: He separates **dispatch paperwork** from physical operation and expects different timing for each.
The **union delegate** is a practical route for checking a repair queue, not a general protest plan.

steps.text: Put dispatch changes on the union safety meeting agenda
Learn the installed AI planning screen and compare repair priorities
Keep operating the haul truck during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2028 means the planning desk changes almost at once, while hands-on robots around 2031 are the bigger threat to our truck shifts. We'd need written safety rules before anyone calls a remote cab a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too short for the younger operators, though my savings and age give me options. I could lose my final well-paid years when robots arrive, and a smaller planning team might weaken the whole crew sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union for a written transition meeting with management, and I'd check the cost of retiring a little early with my partner. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep operating, review any AI dispatch order against pit conditions, and take a real maintenance transfer only if the pay and training are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I could lose some of the income I expected before retirement. I still have enough savings to make choices rather than freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the written offer need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would need the wage, training hours and a safe job description, not a nod in the lunch room. I won't leave a skilled truck post for a promise without numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a younger operator to get the offer in writing before giving up a truck shift. I would ask them to review the wage and training hours with whoever shares their bills.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change planning first, with hands-on truck robots following around 2031.
I would demand **written safety rules** before remote or robot operation changes shifts.
think: I could lose **final high-pay years** once robots reach the truck fleet.
My **savings** give me choices, but younger operators have much less time to build a cushion.
do: **Request** a union-management meeting about written transition rules before AGI arrives.
**Price** early retirement with my partner while the current wage still comes in.
**Review** AI dispatch orders after 2028 and consider maintenance only with written pay and training.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing expected wages before retirement, but I can still plan.
S2.quote: I won't leave a skilled truck post for a promise without numbers.
fieldNote: The **2028 desk change** is immediate for his planning work, while truck replacement is tied to later robots.
He has a **financial exit**, yet insists on written pay and training before accepting a transfer.

steps.text: Ask union delegate for a written transition meeting with mine management
Compare early retirement costs with my partner before deciding whether to leave
Keep operating trucks and check AI dispatch orders against pit conditions
Accept mine maintenance transfer only with written pay and training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people AGI by 2031 gives us five years before the desk work changes and about three more before hands-on robots can run the trucks. That is time to bargain properly, if management starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At my age I might retire before the 2034 robot wave, but I'd hate to leave the junior crew with no training route. My own pay is likely safe for most of the run-up, provided the mine keeps the fleet staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd map my pension dates and ask the union to negotiate paid maintenance training for younger operators. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep leading shifts, check AI work orders, and take a reduced-hours mentoring role only if the wage is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared for my own bills. The extra years let me choose a retirement date instead of being pushed into one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a mentoring role need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a real timetable rather than a ceremonial title. My retirement sums depend on actual hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the fleet shrinks sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs scheduled hours and a rate on paper. A volunteer title won't cover the last part of our retirement plan.

say: **AGI by 2031** gives the mine time to plan before desk changes and the later truck robots.
I would press for **paid training** so junior operators have a route into maintenance.
think: My own **income** looks likely to last through most of the run-up.
The **junior crew** could lose its ladder even if I reach retirement before robot trucks.
do: **Map** pension dates this year against the expected 2031 and 2034 changes.
**Ask** the union to negotiate paid maintenance training for junior operators.
**Keep** leading shifts after 2031 and consider mentoring only with written hours and pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the crew, but able to choose my own retirement timing.
S3.quote: A volunteer title won't cover the last part of our retirement plan.
fieldNote: His **retirement horizon** falls near the robot date, which reduces the risk to his own income.
He uses extra time to seek **paid training** for younger workers rather than assume they can switch unaided.

steps.text: Map pension dates before deciding retirement or accepting paid mentoring work
Ask union to bargain for paid maintenance training for junior miners
Keep leading shifts after 2031 if trucks remain staffed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to make a proper plan, with robot trucks around 2039. The mine should use that runway to train people, not wait for a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when the thinking systems arrive, so my own wage years will mostly be behind me if health and work hold. The issue I carry is whether the younger operators inherit decent jobs and a safe pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep saving from this higher wage and write down the machine faults I teach by ear, so the crew has a usable record. In the first year after 2036 I'd be retired if our planned pension date holds, and I'd advise the union safety group only if they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household money, provided the pension keeps to plan. I'm still bothered by the way a distant deadline can make people postpone training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why write the faults down now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Younger drivers need examples they can use before I leave. I will write down the sound, the truck number and what repair followed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you remain at the mine after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine can show green while the axle makes a noise I know is wrong. My truck fault notes must reach the mine crew before I retire.

say: **AGI by 2036** offers enough time to plan, with hands-on truck robots expected around 2039.
I would ask the mine to start **paid training** well before that date.
think: My own **wage years** should mostly finish before the thinking systems arrive.
I worry that a long runway will let the mine **delay training** for younger operators.
do: **Save** from current high wages and record the equipment faults I teach newer operators.
**Retire** on our planned pension date if our health and savings allow.
feel: I feel **calm** about our income, though the crew’s future still matters to me.
S4.quote: My truck fault notes must reach the mine crew before I retire.
fieldNote: At sixty-eight in **2036**, he expects to be retired if his present plan holds.
He treats **fault knowledge** as a safety asset that should remain with the crew.

steps.text: Keep saving from current mine wages until the planned pension date
Record truck fault sounds while continuing to lead current shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the planning desk could change before we have rules, and robot trucks could cut my final wage years around 2031. A written transition agreement with paid training and clear safety authority would help both me and the younger crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether an operator can stop a truck when a software schedule says keep moving. That right matters more than a glossy training slide.

headlineQuote: A machine can show green while the axle makes a noise I know is wrong.
portrait: **David**, fifty-eight, leads haul-truck loading at a large mine and trusts his ears and crew reports alongside the screens.
His **technical diploma**, senior standing and strong savings give him a realistic route to retirement, with several nearby mines as fallback employers.
He accepts proven tools slowly, uses AI occasionally, and wants **union review** before software reshapes dispatch or repair priorities.
The **2028** scenario threatens his final wage years most; five or ten years give him more room to retire on his terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change mine planning immediately and bring robot trucks around 2031, risking his last high-pay years.
whatWouldHelp: A **written agreement** covering transition pay, paid training and who can stop unsafe truck operations would help.
